newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO delays opening of Bosnian training centre.
newsitem.headline: NATO delays opening of Bosnian training centre.

text.p: The Bosnian federation army has been forced to delay the construction of a U.S.-funded military training centre because the NATO-led peace force has asked to review details of the project, a NATO spokesman said on Tuesday.
The alliance-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) had postponed approving construction of the centre until the federation provides a more detailed account of its plans, officers said.
"SFOR has asked for additional details," said an officer who asked not to be named.

The training centre, located near the western town of Livno close to the Croatian border, is part of a $400 million U.S. military aid programme devised to strengthen Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation army.
An official with the "train and equip" programme said that SFOR had "raised some concerns" about the size of the centre, which would include firing ranges for tanks and artillery.
"They have said it may not be acceptable," said the official, who asked not to be named. "The federation has to make a decision as to the extent of the facility."
Spokesman Colonel Steve Rausch said SFOR headquarters had issued no ultimatum and that the federation's request was under review.
"It just takes time to get these things completely settled," he told Reuters. "The request is working its way through headquarters."

SFOR officers said they expected the training centre to win approval eventually but they insisted that the federation fully disclose its construction and training plans to avoid raising tensions with the rival Bosnian Serb military.
"If everybody knows what's going on up front, things usually go well here," said another officer. "But we're not going to allow something to be slipped through the back door."
The federation intends to construct firing ranges for tanks and artillery at the training centre and to conduct battle exercises for federation battalions, U.S. advisers said.
The "train and equip" programme, which is managed by retired American military officers, presents a delicate matter for the SFOR mission.
The U.S.-led peace force, assigned the task of enforcing the Dayton peace treaty, is keen to present itself as a neutral peacekeeping force which does not favour one army over another.
The "stabilisation" programme is supposed to bring a military balance to the region by bolstering federation forces which were outgunned by the Serbs during the 1992-95 conflict.
European countries and some officers in the peacekeeping mission have criticised the programme, saying it could increase the likelihood of another war.

U.S. advisers in the "train-and-equip" programme and the federation chose the rural site around Livno last year because it allows for training and firing exercises to be held a safe distance from any town.
The opening of the training centre, initially scheduled for the spring, has already been delayed by a dispute among Moslem and Croat federation partners over funding.
The dispute was settled earlier this month, with the Croats agreeing to contribute about $2 million to the $17.5 million project, Western officials said.
